reviews.title: Big Walk Is Unlike Any Other Co-op Game Around, Pushing You to Solve Clever Puzzles With Your Friends by Truly Working Together
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct publisher page verified for Big Walk.
evidence_points: Each of these puzzles rewards us with another red bean we have to take care of as we bring it back to a bean tower for deposit. Once you've found enough beans for a given tower, you get a special key to unlock something new and helpful: stuff you otherwise couldn't figure out how to operate, like a stalled train or an island-spanning chair lift. And in this progression, Big Walk further embeds the ethos that these discoveries are yours to make.

Big Walk's puzzles are always sharp, and always fun. The use of proximity chat makes the process of solving them feel special in a way I haven’t experienced in a game for a long time. Despite the recent wave of co-op games with an emphasis on hanging out with your friends, it feels so new to play in this particular way, as if we were all physically in this virtual space together. Video games often make us feel like superheroes, like the world revolves around our individual characters. In Big Walk, relationships and language are that superpower. The world doesn't revolve around me, but us .

reviews.title: Big Walk review – larking around with mates elevated to an artform
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct publisher page verified for Big Walk.
evidence_points: Switch 2, PlayStation 5, PC; House House The creators of Untitled Goose Game return with an online, open-world adventure that delivers slapstick silliness and bucolic majesty in nearly equal measure
Switch 2, PlayStation 5, PC; House House The creators of Untitled Goose Game return with an online, open-world adventure that delivers slapstick silliness and bucolic majesty in nearly equal measure

So you and up to 12 players step out into this somewhat eerily photorealistic open world to uncover its mysteries. Quickly, you come across challenges which veer from the straightforward to the brain-scrambling: shoot the aforementioned ball-shaped lamp into a hoop; arrange wooden pegs decorated with odd, nature-themed symbols into some kind of shape. For each successfully completed task, you win what looks like a large red peanut. Get enough of these red peanuts and you score a key which in turn unlocks some important piece of infrastructure: for example, a slow-moving, toy-like train whose parping horns are a joy to obnoxiously blare across the otherwise bucolic landscape.

This structure naturally sustains its own rhythm: moments of intense cooperative concentration followed by longer stretches of ambulatory downtime. Such is the layout of this world, you end up doing a lot of backtracking. This is when a little of the game’s quirky lustre wears off since the actual walking is the least interesting part of Big Walk (and you’re also liable to get stuck on bits of rock). Frustration builds as you traipse through the same patch of scrub for the umpteenth time.

Still, Big Walk’s less action-packed moments can be gratifying in their own way: I never tired of watching the twinkling night sky segue with impossible speed into the warm, orange glow of a new day, or stopping to enjoy the sounds of a softly gurgling creek.

The beauty of Big Walk lies in how it tasks you with working together, conversing verbally and physically, to access its most enchanting sights. It stands out in an era when so much of online communication, be that in video games or on social media, has been distorted by a kind of attention-holding logic – for instance, the serotonin-releasing kerching of notifications or the relentless rewards of levelling up. Yet Big Walk eschews these pernicious aspects of digital life for a gentler, less overbearing experience that seems expressly designed to foster enriching connections and childlike playfulness.

Here’s another moment that has stuck with me: wiping away tears of laughter after my brother and I clumsily dropped one of those essential red peanuts to the bottom of the devilishly constructed, practically “ masocore ” 100ft shaft that we had painstakingly platformed our way out of. We nattered about it until we found the next thing that piqued our interest: wobbly rave tunes blaring from deep inside the belly of a mountain. I shan’t say any more: you and your pals will want to discover these delights for yourselves.

reviews.title: Big Walk Is One Of The Best Co-Op Games Ever - GameSpot
2026’s best multiplayer game, properly reviewed by multiple players
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Big Walk.
evidence_points: Today, I take my first steps into a new digital world! I have been tasked with exploring Big Walk , a new co-op game from Untitled Goose Game developer House House. Unlike a recent wave of multiplayer hits that center around shared frustration, Big Walk instead aims to foster chill hangouts in a world full of gentle puzzles that demand close communication between friends. I will not be alone on this expedition. I am joined by my colleagues Julia Lee and Johnny Yu, two navigational experts who have spent hours in the Peak mines . Will the three of us be able to work together and solve the mysteries of a strange world? I’m sure it will go just fine. —Giovanni Colantonio

I spawn into this world not in the vast, open countryside, but in a long hallway. I make my way to the next room to see a big play area with a slide and a jungle gym. I can hear Julia coming down the hall, so I go to surprise her, but instead I am surprised. What is she? Do I look like that? Then Gio comes in. Yes, we all look like some sort of amalgamation of a bug, a duck, and a Chex Mix breadstick. We look a little weird … but it's growing on me. We're just goofy colorful snowmen with legs going for a walk! — Johnny Yu

As we take our first steps, I’m immediately struck by the open world. It has the naturalistic feel of an Elder Scrolls map, but it’s dotted with brightly colored structures that look like they’re constructed out of playground plastic. That contrast makes it easy for us to start mapping out a route as we point out inviting points of interest from the top of an overlook. Even if one of us gets separated from the group, lost out of range from the sensitive proximity chat, we’ll always have landmarks to reconvene at that are visible through the trees. —GC

I lead the charge out of the tutorial area, but realize I can’t hear Julia and Gio anymore. I turn around, flail my arms like a maniac, and jump up and down hoping they can see me. And it works. While the range of Big Walk ’s in-game proximity chat is fairly small, it feels intentional. You're not always meant to hear your fellow breadsticks, so you need to overcome it through gestures. You can flail your arms, give a simple wave, or even punch the ground in hopes that your pals can hear your thumping pleas for help. No matter the method, you'll always end up with your hands raised to the sky after you reunite with your pals or complete a challenge. (Though I wish we could clap our hands). — JY

We stumble into our first puzzle. There is some kind of red shape hanging underneath a blue scaffolding, but it’s too high to reach. Someone remembers that you can pick up another player. Aha! With just a bit of fussing, I am suddenly at the top of a totem pole reaching for a switch. I shout down to the feet of the operation to try and get us positioned right under the button. It takes some awkward communication on my part, but we eventually get on the same page. I click the button, and the vice holding the object loosens, dropping it below. Great! Now what the hell is this thing anyway? —GC

This red bulbous object… I feel maternal to it. It's a make-up sponge? It's a "Kong" dog chew toy? It's a gourd? I shake it, and it sounds like there's something in there, but there isn't much space inside for whatever it is to make noise. I officially decide to call it a "baby," since its segmented form looks similar to our segmented form. I must collect more babies. I should probably also stop shaking them if I'm going to call them babies. —Julia Lee

More puzzles. I get locked in a room full of symbols only I can see, and have to describe them to my friends outside, who have to place cards with those same symbols in the correct order. We find a ball that is too heavy to carry, forcing us to pass it back and forth in relay race fashion to get it to a hole. We discover a straight-up basketball hoop at some point and have to sink enough two-pointers to free the baby. Every puzzle we encounter is different, and plays with team communication in new ways. It’s like navigating one giant escape room splayed across an open-world. Talking over how to solve a puzzle is just as enjoyable as actually executing that solution. —GC

There are a lot of different gadgets and tools scattered around this big island that help us solve these puzzles. Flashlights, a radio, and whatever this doohickey is that marks other items and interactable objects. A lot of them are things that you would naturally bring on a hike or a camping trip. There are tools that help you not get lost, like a map and a compass. There are gadgets that help you communicate with your friends, like a megaphone and walkie-talkies. Everything has its own purpose, with some more obvious than others. Honestly, sometimes it feels like there are too many, because we only have so many hands! For now, I hold onto the flashlight because, man, it really gets dark out here when the sun sets. — JY

I've been put in charge of holding the radio. It's honestly kind of loud and makes it hard to hear my friends sometimes, but I can't resist the soothing music. I'm excited to find out what other radio stations there are to find! —JL
Found a laser pointer. No idea what I can do with it, but I feel compelled to hang on to it for a bit. Surely we’ll find a use for it. —GC

reviews.title: With upcoming PS Plus game Big Walk, Untilted Goose Game developer House House's co-op puzzle quest takes the hangout game to a new peak - here's our review
reviews.identity_evidence: Direct registered professional publisher review verified for Big Walk.
evidence_points: What is Big Walk, exactly? It's a simple game, really, but explaining what's special about it is a little more complicated. For starters, you might wonder if the latest game from Melbourne-based House House is anything like its breakthrough. Well, it certainly shares the gleeful devilment of its biggest hit. There are no geese here, though your colourful avatars do have a somewhat birdlike quality; big or small, that nose is slightly beakish. It's equally smart in the way it wields its silliness, similarly playful and exuberant, and stuffed with innumerable delightful little touches. Otherwise, it's not much like Untitled Goose Game at all.

What it is is a hangout game par excellence, a superior class of what we must apparently now call ‘friendslop' – so, friendgourmet? Friend kino ? It's also a co-operative puzzle game of sorts, designed for small groups; certain elements are retuned for two, three or four players but up to a dozen of you can take part if you have the numbers.
But beneath all that, what it's really about is the frequent joys and occasional frustrations inherent to human communication. (Related: this is my third attempt at writing this intro.)

Big Walk is a little like going on an adventure with your friends while being slightly hard of hearing. By that, I mean its implementation of proximity chat, which is crucial to most things that are great about it, is tuned pretty aggressively – you don't have to venture very far from your mates to find yourself out of earshot. And that's precisely the point: you have the pleasure of larking about together in the wild juxtaposed with the feeling of being alone, whether you actively choose to wander off or simply lose sight of the rest of the group.

That's typical of a game of unlikely contrasts and delightful little frictions. Its world is a sprawling island wilderness pocked with colourful man-made objects and landmarks. This appealingly incongruous mix – purposeful artifice meets untamed nature, the tension between the two lending the place a thrilling sort of liminality – speaks to the game's core principles. Here is a place that's mostly loose and relaxed, with plenty of room to explore or just mooch around, chat amongst yourselves and take in the views. And then there are pockets of space with more focus and purpose to them, where you need to work together as a team to complete the challenges you'll find there.

The curved, red objects that are your reward for solving these collaborative puzzles – vaguely resembling a bottle-gourd, or calabash – are effectively your main form of progression, unlocking a handful of genuinely transformative features. They don't have an official moniker, but our group adopts one after our host decides they look a bit like a certain canine chew toy . The name sticks, and soon it has become part of our shared language, such that no one bats an eyelid when one of us says, "I dropped the kong off the cliff."

Here's the thing: one of you will almost certainly drop the kong off the cliff. It's perfectly round and smooth, and heavier at the bottom, which means one thing: it can and will roll as soon as you set it down. Leave one on the slightest of inclines and within seconds you will invariably find yourself sprinting after it. That's Big Walk for you: if there is an opportunity for mischief, something that will invariably lead to chaos (and perhaps even some mild chastisement for the dropper in this case) then its makers will grasp it with both hands.

Otherwise, this place is largely player-ambivalent. It's never actively hostile, even if at night you instinctively wonder what might be out there – not least since Big Walk's island is clearly modelled on Australia, where a few species of spider are big enough to have their own postcode (fear not, arachnophobes; the only eight-legged creature you'll see is if you form a tower of four). But the presence of a designer's hand always gives something back. There is no need for a detective mode, no need to click in a stick or a trigger to ping the environment when just about everywhere you stand, there is something big and bright to draw the eye, and to orient you.

Meanwhile, when darkness falls, which it does with alarming haste, Big Walk's creators have absolutely no qualms about letting it get really dark. Like Echoes of the Eye dark. Like Dire Marsh (Night) dark. That, of course, is your incentive to carry a light with you. There are torches, yes, but more common are bulbous little lamps – which are also prone to rolling, should you give in to the overpowering temptation to dropkick them. These are perhaps more effectively placed, though, in the circular receptacles scattered across the map, as a helpful reminder to show where you've been. Or, if your group has been separated, a signpost of sorts, pointing the way back to a reunion.

Either way, in Big Walk, you're never truly lost, or at least not for very long. You always have options: you could head for the tower on the top of the nearest hill and launch a firework to tell everyone where you are, or trek back to base and leave a written message on a whiteboard, say, to indicate your imminent whereabouts. Besides, there's a certain frisson to being alone, particularly if you're keen to scare someone. When our group meets back up after a mildly frantic ten minutes apart, we discuss the possibility of setting up a four-player game where one of the group is led to believe it's a three, the fourth cast as a malevolent presence to frighten the wits out of them.

Behind soundproof glass, Tyler is frantically signalling to me by wiggling both his arms over his head. I look over at Morgan, behind a different glass wall, who is holding a puzzle piece over his head—but he can't see Tyler's frenzied arm-swings. I repeat Tyler's gesture, wiggling both of my arms, and Morgan silently gets the message: Wrong piece . He drops it and picks up another.

What's interesting is that in the dozen hours we've been playing first-person co-op puzzle game Big Walk together, wiggling both arms over our heads has meant a number of things and "wrong" is just one of them. It's alternately meant "I've found something" or "come here" or simply "hooray!"

And as well as meaning "wrong," like it does now, it has also meant the complete opposite: "Correct!" That's the genius of Big Walk: it teaches you to communicate with your co-op partners so effectively that you can use the same gesture to mean a half-dozen different things, yet you'll almost always know exactly what your companions are saying. Even when you can't hear them.

Here's how chill the vibes are in Big Walk: there's a tutorial zone where you learn how to jump, crouch, and pick up and use objects, but at no point is there any indication you've finished the tutorial. There's no big arrow pointing at where to go next, or even when to go: we just sort of eventually wandered away from the tutorial and discovered a huge mysterious island waiting for us. No rush.

In our initial wandering we found a tall crane-like structure and eventually noticed it had a button on it, well out of reach. When we figured out how to push that button, we were rewarded with a small poof of confetti and a bulbous red object we decided to call a "nubbin" because it doesn't have a real name. We soon located a slot for that nubbin elsewhere, which led to more puzzles containing more nubbins.
